reels yarın 02.00 , başlık: “What if AI reverse-engineering games is the start of something much bigger?” Caption: “Al is starting to automate one of the most difficult parts of software development: reverse engineering.
Jaden Williams' viral video points to a new wave of Al-assisted game modding where coding agents can inspect existing software, decompile parts of it, identify how it works and help build working modifications.
Tools like Universal Modder now connect agents including Claude Code and Codex with reverse-engineering software such as Ghidra and ILSpy.
The security implications are more nuanced than the video's "death of software" framing.
Making software easier to understand could lower the barrier to finding weaknesses or copying functionality, but reverse engineering a program is very different from breaking modern cryptography or automatically compromising secure systems.
What happens when understanding someone else's software becomes an Al task?

📹: Jaden Williams (@JadenJTW) “

AI / Tech on Instagram: "ChatGPT keeps changing your face?

When editing a photo with AI, small changes in your prompt can make a big difference. The goal is to tell ChatGPT exactly what should change and, just as importantly, what needs to stay untouched.

These prompt shortcuts are designed to make that easier. You can use something like /identitylock when preserving facial features matters, or /poseonly when you want to change the pose while keeping the person consistent.

The same idea can be applied to backgrounds, clothing, lighting, retouching and image quality. Clear constraints give the model less room to reinterpret the original photo.

Save these for your next ChatGPT image edit.

Which one would you use first?

Source: ChatGPT"

AI / Tech on Instagram: "Being rude to ChatGPT might actually work.

A short paper tested 250 prompts on ChatGPT 4o using five different tones, from very polite to very rude. The results showed a small but consistent increase in accuracy as the prompts became less polite.

Very polite prompts averaged 80.8 percent accuracy, while very rude prompts reached 84.8 percent. The study is limited in size, but it suggests that tone alone can influence how an AI model responds.

At the same time, Anthropic has updated its policy to prohibit sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward its models in extreme cases.

So being rude might improve some answers, but AI companies are starting to draw a line around how users treat their models.

Would you change the way you talk to AI for better answers?

Source: Mind Your Tone, Anthropic"
